This is the most boring sci fi game I ever played.

The game follows the classic Bethesda formula, but seems dated in terms of how the quests and stories are structured. The gun play and combat is similar to Fallout 4 and skyrim and doesn't seem to be up to date with other similar titles.

The graphics looks amazing and they have stuck with a more "realistic" sci fi aesthetic rather than futuristic. 

I have played through the majority of the story and done a lot of ship building, colony building and quests  thoughout the known galaxy.

I have always enjoyed Bethesda games and have been a big fan of both the Fallout and Elder Scrolls franchises. I love Sci fi and have played all the major titles across multiple genres such as Mass Effect, Halo, Stellaris, Dead Space, Outer Worlds and X4, so I have experienced a lot of the aspects that Bethesda tries to cover in this game.

Overall it is a very traditional Bethesda game, but doesn't really live up to todays standards. The quests are slow, generic and repetitive. The characters arent that memoriable and unique and the lack of alien races doesn't seem to improve this issue. We have the classic stereotypes with Sarah as a Soldier and Sam as a Cowboy. The most memoriable character seems to be Vasco who is a robot with no story at all.

The colony building seems more limited than in Fallout 4 and you are stuck with the same modules even though you max out your skills - except for some upgrades to mining and some additional decorations.

Shipbuilding doesn't seem that exciting as the basic modules usually makes you end out with a sort of rocket shaped ship and in general the ship designs nudge you towards either a block or a rectangle due to the way the builder forces you to build the ship - the number of modules also seems very limited even though you mix and match between different manufacturers.

Ship combat is somewhat exciting, but you easily get ganged up on by pirates and the game lacks the finesse and flexibility in how you maneuver your craft such as in elite dangerous or X4. This means that space combat very easily becomes a slug fest. where you either target specific parts or have to use specific parts.

Enemy variety is a big issue as well as you have spacers, pirates, cultists and aliens. each have the same behavior and tactics as fallout 4 and are very easy to cheese. The gun play feel sluggish compared to other titles and the guns lack customizability in terms of how they look and feel in combat. For example the old earth rifle looks really weird compared to a normal springfield rifle which seems to be their inspiration. The varuun Starshard seems to be one of the best guns in the game, but it is limited what you can actually do to customize it.

Shipbuilding, colony building and weapon/suit crafting seems to be really important aspects of the game and they have designated quite the number of skills to these elements, but they seem lackluster compared to their importance.

Weapon and Suit variety is also an issue as most suits look the same, laser weapons are limited to orion, solstice and equinox while ballastic weapons have a lot of variety. The rarity system doesn't really make this better as you are constantly looking for the right mix of traits as normal weapons are kind of useless when playing on higher difficulties. the same for the suits.

Capacity is also a big issue in this game. The game wants you to pick up every ressource you find so you can upgrade, research and build, but you have very limited capacity. This leaves you with two options - either go back and forth between your spaceship/base or increase your capacity through the settings (if you have that as an option in your game you know it is bad!). suits, skills and food doesn't really solve this unless you change the setting, so you will spend a lot of time on traveling or constantly having low health.

Mods solve a lot of these issues and a lot of the story mods seems to be better structured and more engaging than the actual in game story - for example the cryomancer or farseer stories. mods that augments shipbuilding and add parts also makes up for this and mods that add different traits or upgrades to weapons and armor has also improved my game.

The only issue being that Bethesda is now taking money for these through their creations shop.

Overall i wouldn't recommend this game unless you want a fallout 4 in space, but with all the down sides of fallout turned up to the max as the game it self hasn't improved any mechanics beyond the graphics.

((Not that they even wrote anything substantial for them anyway from how they move their mouths for about two seconds each, but why put them there like it's a game in pre-alpha that is waiting for them to write something for them and never did? - Major tropes that, at this point, are generic and have all been done hundreds of times over are the main themes of this game, yet it feels like this game is Bethesda trying to be too futuristic for their own good and they suffer from it. Emil Pagliarulo's infamous (lack of) storytelling is on full blast. "Music and light show from magic alien rock then joining some secret society of magic alien rock people" just isn't that interesting the way it's written. I WANTED to like this game. There's so many good aspects of this game where you can see the potential. The New Creation Engine is amazing, the features for gravity, shipbuilding, and space combat feel really good.

People will shit on the engine or the loading screen frequency or any NPC animations, but these are all shallow things that don't affect the actual quality of the game. They're not the problem.

The problem is the questline design, and nothing makes it more clear than those few questlines that are designed well: The UC Vanguard Questline. It's makes such good use of the new engine and mechanics, it has good writing, you can explore a lot of what this game CAN offer.

Then you play anything else, like the main quest. Get thing from planet, go back to New Atlantis. Go to new planet, come back again. They have a huge playground in space that they just don't use. They have a few populated planets each with only one city - a little immersion breaking but I understand the limitations. The problem is they keep making you go between planets for the most inane things. If you're focusing on a questline you rarely stay in one place for long, and when you travel somewhere else there's no excitement or danger: you go through a loading screen to travel then go through another loading screen and another. If it was a loading screen to space and then there was something to do in space before getting to your destination, that would be SOMETHING. The reason everyone points to the loading screens as a flaw isn't because separate cells are unbearable, it's because Bethesda treated most of this game like all their others where everything is one single continuous map with some interiors. The separated maps aren't the fatal flaw, they're merely the lens that exposes the flaw.

This COULD be a good game - if it utilized its own systems and tech upgrades, but it doesn't. The engine feels modern, but the gameplay loop most questlines thrust the player into hasn't caught up. It's a disjointed, incongruous experience that occasionally shows you a 10/10 experience hidden beneath a pile of mediocrity.

One more message specifically for Todd Howard: We play your old games because they're fun to REPLAY and try different builds or factions. Cutting off certain parts of the game for one character based on the player's choices does not limit player freedom, but rather increases and rewards it. Removing consequences from player's choices does not increase player freedom, it renders it meaningless. Stop taking the wrong lessons from your older successes.

Edit: I played 50 hours on gamepass, stop whining about the playtime, Steam is not all-knowing.

In a word: artless. Starfield feels like the natural endpoint of a studio that has been recycling the same approach for twenty years. Everything about it looks ambitious on paper, but the game itself feels like the result of blending scale, procedural generation, and AAA risk-aversion into something strangely empty.

I’ve wanted a proper space game for as long as I’ve been playing games. I love science fiction. I love the fantasy of exploring strange worlds, finding weird little corners of the galaxy, and getting lost in something that feels genuinely unknown. But I think I finally have to accept that this kind of game might never happen at the AAA level. Starfield made that clear.

Because the moment you load into your first planet, you feel the same problem that No Man’s Sky had at launch. When you rely on procedural generation to fill the gaps between handcrafted content, you end up with a lot of space and not a lot of meaning. A hundred empty planets don’t equal one memorable one. And when you try to balance both breadth and bespoke design, the seams show everywhere.

The sad part is that none of this is surprising. Not for Bethesda. Not for AAA.

Bethesda jank used to be charming because the games had personality. The bugs stood on top of something that felt alive. Starfield has the bugs, but the personality is gone. The worlds feel assembled rather than created. The systems feel like they exist because they were on a production roadmap. Ship building. Outposts. Crafting. Factions. A thousand tasks that all blend together into the same gray paste.

This is what happens when a massive team tries to satisfy every possible audience. Too many cooks. Too much money at stake. Too many shareholders who want a game that looks ambitious without taking any actual creative risks. 

The only perplexing thing about Starfield is why they made it at all. Maybe it was the classic trap. The scope was too big. The tech wasn’t ready. The premise demanded bespoke content on a cosmic scale, which is nearly impossible to execute in a way that feels meaningful. When you try to simulate an entire galaxy, you end up with something that feels like a diorama of one.

I wanted to like Starfield. I waited years. The problem isn't unique to Starfield, it's AAA in general. You either get a giant open world packed with shallow systems, or you get a highly scripted roller coaster that barely feels like a game. There’s very little in between.

The silver lining is that indie games are better than ever. Maybe that’s where the real experiments will keep happening. Maybe that’s where someone will finally make a space game worth getting lost in.

It just isn’t this one.

If I had to pick one word to use for Starfield, it would be "unfortunately". The core game is good, technology wise the game is the best yet aside from one minor bug I found very early that was easily resolved. The loading screens are an unfortunate result of the game engine's age, but the game looks pretty and you can get some really great views from it.

However this is not where the game falls down, for all it's technical accomplishments (and for the game engine, it really is especially the ship building stuff) the game is fatally holed by the universe. Someone hilariously and depressingly summed it up as "Space America vs Space Texas" and this couldn't be more true. The background lore is generally bland, and is disappointingly not expanded upon when it isn't. That's ignoring the bits that don't make sense under the mildest scrutiny.

The story's version of "exotic" is anyone with an accent, and they can veer too close to the stereotype sun, so it too often feels a bit uncomfortable or bordering on parody. The main companions are better, but there is too little variety in their outlook - what flavour of "Lawful Good" would you like today?

The main mission is terribly bland and like the rest of the game full to the brim with missed opportunities - why does each new universe mean so little? Why are there so many powers when most are rubbish and/or poorly explained? There was a golden opportunity to make comparisons with the Hunter as you - the player - start to see each universe as a stepping stone and become more detached from the people in it. Or even put the extra effort in for very minor visual changes each universe that help make it feel more meaningful. Can't even be bothered give a character a different hair style?

The game has a great visual feel to it (Space Texas aside), but even this lacks cohesion. There's some posters for war veterans getting cybernetic limbs - cool.  Is there any other mention of this, does anyone have a cybernetic limb? No. Planets look great, and seeing other planet and moons in the system doesn't get old. Sadly I can't say the same for how sparse all of them are, exploring to see the same thing you've seen countless times before.

The character customisation is good at its core, but - surprise - unfortunately it is let down by the clothing and suit options. You're really reduced in choice, with just a body and head for clothing and the space suit gets a backpack on top - there's no crafting just (reduced) upgrade options. Trying to get a decent suit set is like gambling as you raid chests and boss corpses hoping for something that doesn't suck (it will). That's before you want a matching set... Coming from other Bethesda games this is a huge downgrade and an even bigger let down. Fallout 4 had gibbing in, but that's missing too despite the bigger and nastier space guns here. Why are we getting so much less in a newer game?

The random POIs are good in theory, but there are far too few. I very quickly memorised them and knew where to look and what to find, it makes the game wear on you sooner than it should. There needs to be at least twice as many, ideally many more.

This game doesn't know what it wants to be. Clearly, Bethesda was inspired by No Man's Sky but the open world nature of that game conflicts with Bethesda's strengths as a studio. The procedural generation of the planets results in content which commits the cardinal sin of gaming, which is that it is BORING. There are a few scattered points of interest, and some resources to gather and animals or plants to scan and that's basically it. NMS has all kinds of interesting things to find but not here. Plus the fact that you have to scan objects multiple times is just pointless busy work.

You do get the signature Bethesda RPG features like fully voice-acted dialog but, honestly, who cares? Who is actually listening to all of this? It worked in Skyrim because there are a lot more interesting characters and the world is more flavorful but here, IDK, I just did not really care about most of the characters I met and most of your companions are so goody two shoes and bland.

The combat is okay - it is serviceable at at least. Some of the extended quest lines are not bad. And the ship building is decent if kind of generic. My main issue with the gameplay is that Bethesda didn't commit to their own mechanics. You can mine and extract resources but they can all be bought so cheaply from basically anywhere that there is little point. You can build a base but your ship has all the features anyways so what is the point? And again, that's because the game doesn't know what it wants to be - it has some of the gathering-crafting mechanics of NMS but they feel relatively pointless. Some of the quest lines are pretty good but the core of the game is extremely generic and lazily implemented procedurally generated worlds which are boring and stale and just not fun to run around. In my opinion, it would have been better if they had concentrated on a more limited number of planets which were more densely populated with content and locations. This mish-mash of survival game, procedural generation, and hand-written quests just does not come together. It is like a bunch of disjointed parts that don't play well together.

And though I didn't ever get there, the NG+ mode is not a good fit for a game like this. You spend dozens of hours building bases and ships, finding the best gear, and doing all the quests and you want me to do it all over again, just with my better skills and abilities? Yeah, no thanks - I have no interest is resetting my progress. This is yet another feature that just seems tagged on which doesn't work well with the whole.

I will say that I did have some fun with this game and it has its merits. But for most of these boxes they were trying to check off here, you'd be better off playing No Man's Sky, which does "endless" space, procedural generation, and survival-crafting extremely well. There are also minimal loading screens - dear god, don't get me started with the ludicrous number of loading screens in Starfield. It's absurd.

It looks nice, and I do appreciate the "NASAcore" aesthetic, but there's just not a lot that's compelling in this game.
The main quest starts of okay, loses steam in the middle, and ends in a nonsensical way.
The companions you can have with you all have mostly flat personalities that didn't compel me to have any particular one stay with me.
The different planets are mostly barren randomly-generated wastelands, and that kills any real sense or desire for exploration.
The gameplay is basic but usable, generally what you expect from a Bethesda game.
Space flight/combat is cool, but is hardly present in the overall flow of the game, and the way travel from different locations works, you'll just end up fast-travelling most of the time anyway.
The non-randomly-generated locations are hit and miss, but some of them are actually pretty cool.
Building you own ship is actually relatively fun after you get used to the UI.
All in all the game is okay, but not worth the full price I paid for it, and I'm not excited for any DLC or sequels.

Starfield is a poorly designed game, coupled with critical bugs that show an absolute disregard for the customers who purchased the game. 

Every encounter is with dozens of enemies who always have the high ground, and frequently surround you. When fighting at long range, the computer has perfect accuracy on shots, frequently ignores cover, and combines that with invisible walls that turn hits into misses every time. Enemies are also complete bullet sponges. 

This game's definition of "difficulty" is built around this combination of bugs left carefully in place, and conscious design decisions built around attritional difficulty. The game literally designs single encounters to run you out of medpacks. 

As with combat, exploration is tedium combined with unfixed bugs, 2 years after the game's release. Environmental hazards are jacked up such that getting out of your ship and walking 100 meters has you already taking damage. This is, again, combined with encounters of a dozen or so opponents, who have the high ground and their (I assume this is at least purposeful) unerring long-range accuracy. 

The combination of a bug causing the planet's environment to ignore my suit, and remove my boostpack, while simultaneously inflicting poison damage, while I was being attacked by a dozen zealots was on one of the first missions of the entire game. 

I am almost embarrassed to admit that I played this game to completion, because I had to see if it got better. This is the company that gave us Skyrim after all, one of my favorite games. I couldn't believe the game would actually stay THIS BAD.

In fact, the final mission in the game was actually worse. Enemies that can spawn endless duplicates of themselves (with rocket launchers, naturally), who teleport away every time you attack them, and run you through one shooting gallery after another (I believe there are six total shooting galleries) all in a bid to, again, run you out of healing. That's right, the game has MULTIPLE encounters like this. 

This game has that Bethesda magic in spots, as long as you are only doing procedurally generated missions. The moment you engage with either the main story, or a faction questline, you will be subjected to numerous attritional encounters, where bugs combine with stunningly bad, unfixed bugs. 

This game has no respect for you or your time, nor does it really seem to give a damn if you have fun. It is without a doubt the worst Bethesda game ever, and I have played every game they have developed since Morrowind. 

If you're considering buying this game on a holiday sale, as I did, do yourself a favor and skip it. No matter the price, you could find something better to spend it on.

Starfield is haunting.

It's a beautiful, expansive canvas, a labor of astonishing love for science-fiction, astronomy, and humanity. And upon this canvas is sketched the most bare framework of a game.

Or perhaps *stretched* is the better word; what's basically happened is that all the elements of Fallout 4 or Skyrim have been pulled apart, quite literally, and laid across a thousand planets rather than given context in their relative placement in a theme-park world, like previous Bethesda games. You aren't distracted and pulled from curious thing to strange location as you work your way toward an eventual destination, but instead hopping directly to wherever it is you "want" to go.

The lack of context really hurts the content on offer. Some of the best quest writing and environmental design in any Bethesda game is severely let down by its meaningless, randomized placement on otherwise dead worlds. The "lore" feels much more shallow because the cartoony character of the economics and politics at play is so much more obvious when planted in the middle of endless, unexploited wilderness.

And all of these problems are relatively minor in comparison to my real problem: the game feels like it's actively admonishing the player for playing it. The core conflict in the main story is set up to critique the same activities the game encourages the player to engage with... by being the *only* activities available. You will kill six thousand space pirates, whether or not it's logical that that many even exist, because you have no other choice if you want to play the game, and the game will call you evil for doing that. The ending will, incredibly, make this feel even worse.

A more constrained game could pull all this off. By assigning the player a character, or by narrowing the scope of their explorations, a more pleasant experience could be possible (and indeed has been, in games like Freelancer, Mass Effect, Rogue Trader, or Spec Ops: The Line). But Starfield intends to capture the eerie sensation of the desolate universe we find ourselves in, instead, and has tried to strap another game to that experience.

Starfield is haunting because it almost achieves what it sets out to do, and then hobbles itself. I can't help but imagine what it might've been.

All my waxing philosophical aside, you can get a couple hundred hours of decent fun out of this thing if you're willing to put up with some pain points. The combat is good! The environments are astonishing! There's a lot of cool things out there! They're just too far apart for most people to appreciate, and for every great quest there's a dozen of the same, identical outpost full of space pirates inexplicably having a picnic on an airless moon.

If you’re willing to spend $70 on what amounts to a watered-down, space-themed version of Skyrim—without truly feeling like the main character—then this game may be for you. Dialogue often feels antagonistic, with NPC interactions that lack warmth or meaningful engagement.

One of the few genuinely compelling features is shipbuilding. The customization system allows for impressive creativity, including recreations inspired by other sci-fi franchises. Unfortunately, this strength is not enough to carry the overall experience.

Much of the gameplay feels like a re-skin of mechanics from Fallout and The Elder Scrolls. While that familiarity could have been a positive, it instead highlights how little innovation there is. The game evokes comparisons to DayZ in space, but without the benefit of unique or memorable environments.

The New Game Plus mechanic is an interesting concept, but its execution is disappointing. After completing the main story and side quests, there is little incentive to replay when progress, equipment, and even meticulously built ships are lost—with no option to save or preserve custom designs. Rebuilding everything from scratch quickly becomes tedious rather than rewarding.

Overall, the game has moments of potential, but they are overshadowed by repetition, lack of meaningful progression, and design decisions that undermine long-term replay value.

A game full of missed potential.

I’ve been playing Bethesda games since Morrowind. Back in the good ol' days where installing mods required only having WinZip installed. Now look at mods like the mod that adds hair and cape physics to Skyrim SE. It’s dependency nightmare and mod manager shenanigans.

I’ve played Arena and Daggerfall as well, unlike most TES fans. I’ve played Fallout 1 and 2, unlike most Fallout fans.

I like Bethesda games. A lot. I enjoy the gameplay loop. I enjoy modding the heck out of them. So, once Starfield finally went on a sale that I found acceptable, and after being disappointed with New Vegas, the game the community overhypes as the best Fallout (it’s Fallout 3 that’s the true best, in my opinion), I figured it was time to try it out.

Ohh boy.

This is a brand new universe, IP, franchise for Bethesda. Elder Scrolls games start you off slow and easy and if you’re interested in the world, there’s tons of lore books scattered around. Fallout games usually start with the “War… War Never Changes” guy giving you a brief recap of how the world got the way it is. Starfield has none of these things. I had no clue about the history of this universe until I stumbled upon the UC Vanguard faction questline, which briefly recaps how Earth lost its atmosphere and the subsequent events that followed. Why wouldn’t the game open up with this?

Then you are given a ship just because and you end up joining Constellation; a faction of explorers looking for artifacts. This faction also has the four most annoying and insufferable companions of all Bethesda games. Granted, most companions in Bethesda games are either just there (Oblivion, Skyrim) or approach Bioware-level greatness yet don’t fully live up to that potential (FO3, FONV, FO4). Here, all the companions share the same morals and ethics. Every time you do something in a questline that they don’t like, the game will interrupt you as these companions lecture you about your choice. In a game where you’re encouraged to be and do whatever you like. Bethesda thought it was great that companions will berate you and chastise you whenever you don’t play the way they prefer.

Then there’s the outpost building mechanic. In FO4, the Settlement system worked well enough, but it was too clunky to use for extended periods. Installing Sim Settlements is basically a mandatory step to fix this, because as the tradition goes, you gotta install mods to fix stuff Bethesda just left there. Here, there’s no such mods, instead, there’s a few helpful ones like the Universal Stash mod that are, in my opinion, mandatory to enjoy this game. The problem with outposts is that you’re encouraged to have many of them in order to have them grind materials you’ll need for research projects and weapon/spacesuit mods. Well, getting all the materials transported from 8 outposts to the one you want is a logistical nightmare. Why couldn’t they all just share the same inventory? No, you have to “ship” a limited number of materials to the outpost you select, eventually setting up an overly complex supply chain. Dude, this is a western RPG, not Victoria 3 or Anno 1800. It needs to be simpler than this.

All this aside, you install mods to fix the game and make it more bearable, and what’s this? Why does my character look like the Michelin mascot? Because, Bethesda, when given the chance to work on a brand new IP, they choose “NASA punk” as the aesthetic. I could not deal with this at all. So, I waited until there were mods to fix this. Do yourself a favor and install KZ Tachyonic Core Arsenal and KZ Aggregation of Scraps for some actual attractive Mass Effect-like space suits.

Then, as you play, you’ll find an Astra, a rare material that if you have three, you can exchange it to get a random Legendary item. Kind of like a gacha game except you get the currency as you play. Not bad. I amassed around 13 Astra and let’s get some loot…. oh, the loot table is broken because I started the Freestar Rangers questline. How does this even happen? Apparently this bug has been here since before Shattered Space came out, and it still hasn’t been fixed. So instead of the loot table having everything, it only has Loredo branded weapons and a few spacesuit types. So, Astra are now worthless… until installed the McClarens Outfitters mod that lets me remove Legendary effects from armor and apply it on the armor of my choice. With 1 Astra, it lets you duplicate items and even upgrades them to the next tier. It’d be nice if I could do it for weapons too… oh you can! But you have to do a gigantic grind to get to modify your weapons too with this mod. So, not even modders can get this game design right. I don’t get what’s so hard about this.

“Dude, stop ranting, hows the story?” Warning, spoilers ahead! [spoiler] Well… it’s barely a story. I don’t tend to like stories in most Western RPGs, I’ve realized. I seem to have the most fun with JRPG and VN storylines. That said, it’s an okay sci-fi story about exploration and space anomaly shenanigans. The plot twist would have been decent, if I didn’t see it coming from miles away. It’s entirely too predictable and the way they choose which party member gets to die is ridiculously stupid. Bethesda chose the top 2 party members you always use and put them into a dangerous situation where you must pick who to save. If I knew this beforehand, I would have used Sam and Barret exclusively since I don’t like them. Heck, I don’t like Sarah or Adreja either. This whole sequence just felt bland and empty to me.

Then there’s the whole “Unity” thing. You lose all your gear and items, and you essentially start a new game+ with your level, perks and abilities intact. New things happen during this mode as well. The reason I bring it up is because during this sequence, you get to hear your character talk, and it reminds me of the best feature of Fallout 4; the voiced protagonist. It seems people vastly prefer playing as a mute. I don’t understand how that aids in roleplaying in anyway. To think, a universe where Starfield has a voiced protagonist. Now that’s a universe I’d make a Unity Jump for. [/spoiler]

The combat is pretty much Fallout 4 without VATS and with Dragon Shouts. That pretty much sums it up. It’s a lot of fun, and I love fighting legendary enemies to get that loot. The loot system is improved from Fallout 4. It’s closer to Diablo now. Blue tier items are rare and have one special effect. Purple tier items are Epic and have two special effects. Yellow tier items are Legendary and have three special effects. It’s satisfying. 

My favorite companion was the Adoring Fan. I think that says it all. 

I liked this game, and I will play more of it in the future. I still haven’t finished the UC Vanguard, Freestar Rangers and Shattered Space questlines yet. But, it seems like loop I have for this game is excitement and then disappointment and then fix with mods. And, after 105 hours, I feel exhausted. I want to play a game that “just works” out of the box, Todd. Right Todd?

Planet layouts are procedurally generated, which makes exploration pointless since you will encounter environments with random permutations of the same assets and textures. The result is, most of the time, an empty wasteland with one or two bandit outposts here and there and some creatures roaming around if you are lucky.

Perks are insignificant, they will give you pathetic bonuses with next to no impact on your gameplay. Outside of perks that allows you to upgrade the space ship, the sense of skill progression is nonexistent in this game making the whole RPG aspect almost void.

Player agency is very limited, turning a lot of dialogue choices into variants of "Yes". The main story could be worse and some of the side quests (including faction questlines) are really interesting. That being said, most characters have the personality of a wet cardboard and are extremely one dimensional.

Spaceship and base building are fun but lack a sense of purpose. The only benefit you get from customizing your ship is the distance you can fast travel at. It makes no difference in regards to space combat as you will have an equally easy time destroying enemy ships, because again, there is no challenge in the combat system.

I don't hate Starfield nor do I think it the worst game, I mean I'm installing it again as I write this review, but I can't say it successfully hooked me in. The things I love most in a bethesda game aren't (or weren't when I played its been a few months) present and in most cases it would make more sense to go and play Skyrim.

I've seen enough. Here's my opinion:

This game has a very solid base, and a lot went into the world building and design. But all of that falls short with the technical aspects. I don't know how to explain it, but this game feels like something from 15 years ago. Controls feels dated, ai feels incredibly dumb, gunplay feels boring and also dated. Leveling is way too simple and straight forward for this type of rpg. Followers are forced at the beginning and they are annoying as hell. They get in your way, get stuck on tables, take a seat in mid air and engage in the classic Fallout/Skyrim clunky combat. You are bombarded with info dumps from all sides, and it is quite overwhelming.

And then there is the story and quest system. Again, it feels old, uninspired and at the same time convoluted. Go talk to this person, join this group, go grab some random item from a pirate infested ship, etc. A lot is thrown at you, while you're still trying to get a grasp of the game. I got no less than 10 random non-related quests added to my journal by me just walking around the city, while my companion is talking to me constantly, and others try to do the same. All of the sudden I am loved and I'm surrounded by people that want me in their guild. I don't want that. I don't feel like I have a reason to do those things, and the dialog options always force you into a certain path. "Oh yeah, random miner, have my ship for no reason. You're amazing, go here and join this group of space explorers and become their favorite guy." "Oh, hi! Welcome to the Companions. Have a 4 star suite and join in our conversation!" "I think you should have the honor of placing this chunk of metal on our floaty hologram doohickey. You've done so much for us" (said the lady that I just met 10 minutes ago)

Then there is the massive amount of systems and mechanics that you're trying to learn, as the story forces you to keep going forward. Like, let me breathe! I don't want to travel to that planet/moon, etc. Not yet. I arrive at Mars, and not even 5 minutes later, that lady whose name I forgot, already wants me to jump in the ship and go to a different system, then to a random station, and then to some derelict ship. I don't even know what 90% of the ship's systems do, or how they should be handled, because a mini tutorial was thrown at me in the middle of a battle and some lady trying to talk to me about some group I don't care about.

Why do I need a spacesuit, if I can walk naked out in a planet with no oxygen and not die? Why do I have fuel if it never runs out, and I can travel wherever I want to? Why do I have a carry weight limit if I never get encumbered? Have I ran into a bug? Why do I have an option to sell items from my ship, but I get zero items listed, when I know they are in my ship's locker?

But anyway, another thing that really bothers me: This is a soft sci-fi/fantasy world, so why the hell am I stuck being a human, and there's only humans all around the universe? Where's the aliens? There should be different races, with different abilities, perks, etc. Speaking of which, the character design is horrendous. There aren't many CC options that even let you be however you want to look. Everyone looks blocky and... ugly.

Performance wise, this game runs great on my end. Experiences might vary. The game looks okay, but it doesn't hold to modern standards. It looks like Fallout 3 with texture and lighting enhancements. As mentioned before, the game looks and feels old.

Sound is terrible. While the music is great, sound effects are incredibly weak. Gunshots are very silent.

Controls are stiff, yet too snappy at the same time. You are either too slow or too fast.

Enemies are bullet sponges. And I get it that it is an rpg, but this is why I hate guns in rpg's. It makes for very unrealistic gunplay, when I have to unload two magazines into an enemy's face so they die.

Flying in space is pointless. I get what they were going for, but it doesn't work for a game. There is nothing out there. The scale is realistic, but it serves no purpose. You can't directly land in a planet either. They are a gigantic low poly balls with no collisions, and it will; literally take you real life days to get from one to the other without fast travelling.

I can go on, but I think I've mentioned everything that there is to be mentioned. I'll mod this game to hell, and see if that improves the experience. Vanilla = Not worth it.

I really wish I could give this a neutral review. I have a lot of things I absolutely despise about it but also it's still a very fun game and shooter, and in some ways the space RPG I've wanted since I was a kid. Here's to hoping it will actually be some day. I will still be playing it (WITH MODS), but I absolutely do NOT recommend spending $70 on it.

I'm gonna start with the cons since they kinda overshadow the good.

Cons:

- The writing for the most part is god awful, at least for the main story. Literally "Uh, he's right behind me isn't he?" levels of writing. Feels like a PG-13 marvel movie set in space, yet somehow feels like you're being talked down to the entire time. I can't stand pretty much every single one of the main companions you get in the game, with the exception of Vasco. (I love Vasco so much and if you hurt him great harm will befall you.) So I tend to avoid the main quest, because the dialogue is just really bad and not a fun way. The concept is cool, but that's about it.

- The amount of loading screens and screen transitions for everything from leaving buildings to leaving a planet to traveling between planets and systems is insane. I feel like a large portion of my gameplay so far has been navigating menus, probably close to 50% of my game time. I've heard they're fixing this early 2026 so I'll edit this review when that's done.

- Settlements are as of this review (Jan 2026) pretty barebones. Coming from Fallout 4 it feels like they took a significant amount of steps back.

- The cities still feel pretty lifeless and incredibly small. Neon is the size of a small shopping mall. Like, I'm pretty sure I've seen interior locations in Fallout bigger than Neon. Akila City and New Atlantis are slightly bigger than Neon but they're maybe the size of a medium-sized hold from Skyrim at most. I know a lot of humanity was wiped out by the Colony Wars and leaving earth but come on dude the capital city of the UC shouldn't be the size of a suburb.

- I enjoy exploring planets, I just think the walkable area needs to be much larger and the POIs much further apart. No reason I should land on some random remote part of an uninhabited PLANET and see a bunch of factories and bases not even 1km apart, especially outside of settled space. Unfortunately that requires making planets more interesting in general, and I have no ideas on how to do that other than making it seem less like a randomly generated terrain box with little to nothing in the distance and more like you're actually exploring an entire planet. Maybe upgrade the fauna AI so you can do some more in-depth Xenobiology? Random interesting weather events you can document? Strange anomalies?

Pros:

- Customization is really good, still wish we had the option to mix and match bottoms and tops. Still not a thing in Bethesda games I guess lol.

- The aesthetic of the game is great, love the NASA-punk theme and the graphics (with some HDR tweaks) are absolutely beautiful. But I just have to say, please do something about the characters having completely dead eyes even when they smile. It's a little uncanny-valley.

- The ship building is really fun, I wish there were a little more options available to really make your ship yours (decals, hab shape variants, etc.) but it's still fun. I love making my ship cozy and just chilling in there out in the middle of space.

- Gunplay is really great in my opinion, better than Fallout 4 even. I could spend hours and hours getting into shootouts with pirates and spacers and it's fun every time. Fast paced but with room to be as tactical as you want, especially in higher difficulty settings.

- People tend to be really mixed on this, but I like the ship combat personally. It's a little simple but it gets the job done and feels responsive enough. Actually feels like you're flying a giant space boat, and you can really feel when you fire your guns, especially the cannons. Sound effects are great too, though I think if Bethesda is aiming for realism with the NASA-punk aesthetic they could make space truly silent unless you're in the cockpit, with maybe just some reverberation of the hull or deep rumbles or something. Also, we all want space walks. NMS has it now, Starfield still doesn't.

- This game captures the loneliness of what I imagine space travel to be like really well about 75% of the time. I love wandering around a planet after a couple shweezies of the beezy and getting lost imagining what it must be like to watch a different sun set on a different world. The strange nature sounds on lush planets, the muffled sounds on planets with low atmospheres, the strange and almost uncanny silence on a moon orbiting a massive gas giant. Makes you feel really small in a good way, but again I hope they expand upon terrain generation. It's pretty much all the same as of right now, I want to be able to wander into different biomes.

- The modding community is going strong and there are plenty of great mods out there to improve upon what Bethesda's done with the base game.

- There are genuinely plenty of different ways to play the game and make it YOUR space story, which in my opinion is what makes it a great RPG. As I've mentioned before, I hate the writing in the main questline so I've started doing anything from Xenobiology on one character to being a bounty hunter on another, to being a space trucker, to a chem dealer on Neon. It does allow for plenty of play styles, and I'm hoping Bethesda expands upon this even more.

Summary:

Overall, wait for a sale. It's a fun game you can put hundreds of hours into but it's not the best Bethesda game by any means. The issues are frustrating and strange, but what the game gets right it really gets right. The potential is there though, and I'm really hoping this eventually becomes THE space RPG. Also please hire better writers, Bethesda. Where'd your Fallout and Skyrim team go?

Starfield is a game that does some things right and some things wrong. Unfortunately, the things it does wrong make it hard to love.

The positives: The dialogue system is a real step up from Oblivion, Skyrim and especially Fallout 4, and you are actually able to talk your way through a few quests this time around. It's not quite New Vegas in terms of role playing potential, but a giant step in the right direction, that I don't think Bethesda get enough credit for having taken. The world building and environmental storytelling is pretty good in parts. Gun play is decent, and ship building is really quite fun.

The negatives: Well, have you heard about the repeated locations? There is little reward for exploring planets once you have seen the vast majority of the possible locations, which I managed to do well under the 100 hour mark. Characters are bland and uninteresting and the story feels very "meh". Most aspects of the game feel very much like they were designed by a bunch of committees rather than stemming from the visions of a few creative individuals — everything is safe, sterile, boring and "corporate" as a result. I think the skill system actually is a little bit better than the perk system in Fallout 4, at least in theory, but in practice many of the skills are pretty unimaginative, and can be a real drag to grind. Building outposts is a real bore compared to building settlements in Fallout 4, and even though they dumbed down the construction options a lot, it somehow still manages to be just as buggy as it was in that game, and forget getting Bethesda to do anything about it. Flying your spaceship is a combat-only experience; there's nothing interesting to discover out in space, and you can mostly just skip having to pilot your ship altogether by fast travelling.

Hours Played: Enough to explore planets.. and wonder what’s on the next one
Verdict: ⚠️ Mixed‑Positive (Epic Scope, Uneven Delivery)

Starfield is Bethesda’s bold leap into space RPGs: huge galaxy, hundreds of planets, ship building, deep RPG progression, and plenty of sci‑fi quests. If you love exploration, RPG freedom, and building your own narrative as a galactic adventurer, there’s a lot here to sink your teeth into. The universe is massive, factions are varied, and many quests feel genuinely engaging.

That said, the execution isn’t flawless. Planet exploration can feel repetitive and sometimes empty, with long travel between systems breaking immersion. Procedural generation means some planets feel similar, and combat, NPC animations, and storytelling can feel rough or dated compared with other modern RPGs.

What Starfield does right:

* Huge, varied universe to explore
* Deep RPG systems and ship customization
* Fun quests and faction content
* Epic scale that feels like a space adventure

Where it struggles:

* Repetitive/exploration loops and empty planets
* Loading screens that interrupt flow
* Dated animations and some technical roughness
* Story and worldbuilding not as engaging as expected

Starfield is a sprawling game with massive ambition and moments of real wonder, but it also has noticeable rough patches and design quirks that divide players. If you dream of piloting ships, joining factions, and charting star systems and can overlook some bumps along the way there’s a lot of enjoyment here. Otherwise, be prepared for a slower, more uneven ride through the cosmos.

The RPG aspect of the game is good, ship building is great, and the story/setting felt boring.

Biggest gripe is in-fact the loading screens. If you're the player who just fast travels everywhere then this is a non-problem. If you're the player that likes to play slow and explore, then this becomes a problem.

Why? Getting into your spaceship = loading screen, launching or landing your spaceship = loading screen, flying to different planets or systems = loading screen, even traveling between city areas = loading screen. While yes, this is how all Bethesda games pretty much go, Starfield amplifies this problem due to the pure fact that your main means of travel is a spaceship, and that you're constantly traveling between planets and star systems. You can technically fast travel from planet to planet, which reduces your loading screens significantly, but if you intend to use your space ship at all, then prepare to get disappointed that 90% of your spaceflight is loading screens.

That's honestly my second biggest gripe; while the spaceship builder is great, actual use for your spaceship is severely limited other than a means to interact with loading screens. The only time you can actually fly your spaceship is in orbit of another planet, but you cannot travel between planets without going into the menu, selecting the planet you want to go to, watch a short animation into a loading screen, and then you're place right in orbit of the planet. So I do not recommend this game at all if one of the main appeals of this game to you is flying a spaceship, because while the actual flying of the spaceship felt fine, there's very little reasons to even bother since you cannot fly anywhere out of orbit of the planet you're at.

I have mixed feelings on this game. I love space, so that gives it most of its pull for me. Plus, Bethesda is a pretty good studio for the most part, though I do have some thoughts on how lazily some aspects of their games are put together because they know people will write it off as 'Bethesda Jank' or let the modders fix it.

That being said, if you're going into this thinking it'll scratch your space exploration itch - Don't. It's not worth it. Exploration is repetitious and dull, finding the same POIs in the same proc-gen landscapes. While the occasional POI is interesting, it simply is not enough to save the game. Space flight is a glorified loading screen, too. Piloting the ships feels fine, but actual ship combat is quite dull. Aside from the fact that there simply isn't much to do in space, you'll mostly spend time accessing your map to move to a different system, where you can then access your map to land on a planet. Space exploration is as wide as an ocean, but as deep as a puddle. If you want actually interesting gameplay in space, I advise playing No Man's Sky or Elite Dangerous. Even EVE has more fascinating space gameplay, and that game is just Microsoft Excel.

So, how are the quests? Well... They're okay. For the most part, storylines of side quests are serviceable. There are some highlights that have stuck with me from the occasional quest, but it's mostly forgettable. Beyond that, even the quests that ARE good will often feature a choice in quest design that either confuses or angers you. Take for example the quest where you have to choose to release an experimental bio-weapon with a chance of mutating and attacking humans or bringing a creature back from extinction that would serve the same purpose as the bio-weapon, but over a longer scale. So, if you're like me, you'd assume that gambling on a bio-weapon isn't the ideal outcome. That's not what your companions think. At worst, they chide you for not being forward-thinking enough, and at best they hand-wring about how 'it doesn't seem like the right choice'.

The main story itself is utterly dull, which isn't necessarily new for Bethesda. But for a game that espoused its 'awesome New Game+', you think there would be more motivation to actually finish the main quest. Speaking of the New Game+ mechanic, it's similarly shallow. There are a wide variety of changes that can occur, but hardly anything that will keep you interested enough to complete another playthrough.

The gunplay is fun, but it's dragged down by the classic Bethesda artificial difficulty of bullet sponges. Of course, guns aren't your only weapon. You're also given access to a variety of powers that your character 'shouts' to activate--

Yeah, everybody knows about the Dragonborn in space shit. It's egregious, barely justified by the plot and genuinely laughable. I think Skyrim's success broke Todd Howard's brain. The powers themselves are fine. They can be fun, but never quite as interesting or enjoyable as Skyrim's shouts. Partly because you've played this exact game before, just in a medieval high-fantasy setting instead.

Companions are basically cardboard cut-outs. They do have quests, but they're rarely interesting. I found Sam to be the most enjoyable one, and that was only because he was supplemented by his daughter, Cora. Together, they make about 2/3rds of an interesting character (though that itself might be a generous figure).

So, I've been pretty harsh, but is Starfield worth it? Short answer - No. It's not worth £59.99. 

At most, I'd recommend spending around ~£30 on the game, and that's only if you REALLY enjoy Bethesda's formula and are into space games enough to keep you chugging to the finish line. Even if that was the game's asking price, my review would still be negative. Bethesda released a below-standard game at their usual asking price, talking it up as an 'exciting new IP' but there's little worth here. I was willing to give it a chance, and dumped a not-insignificant amount of hours into the game. From my 126 hours, I came to realise Starfield's biggest crime. 

You constantly think the game is on the verge of getting good.

Each main quest, each side quest, each new system - There are just enough good ideas and concepts there to present something interesting and worth exploring. But time and time again, Starfield will show a flashy intro and then promptly fall on its face, breaking its nose and chipping its teeth. Yet, it'll stand back up and perform an impressive flourish, just enough to make you think, 'Oh, okay. We're getting into it for REAL this time!' And then Starfield falls again. 

The main quest always feels like you're on the verge of something interesting happening, but it never does. The side quests will occasionally have fascinating set-pieces, introductions or concepts, but they never land the execution. 

Ultimately, there is nothing to be gleamed from Starfield. It'll only make you look at Bethesda with a more bitter outlook on their formula and the games that came before. I have little hope in TES6 or Fallout 5, or any other game Bethesda chooses to work on (god forbid they make Starfield 2).

This is the most boring sci fi game I ever played.

The game follows the classic Bethesda formula, but seems dated in terms of how the quests and stories are structured. The gun play and combat is similar to Fallout 4 and skyrim and doesn't seem to be up to date with other similar titles.

The graphics looks amazing and they have stuck with a more "realistic" sci fi aesthetic rather than futuristic. 

I have played through the majority of the story and done a lot of ship building, colony building and quests  thoughout the known galaxy.

I have always enjoyed Bethesda games and have been a big fan of both the Fallout and Elder Scrolls franchises. I love Sci fi and have played all the major titles across multiple genres such as Mass Effect, Halo, Stellaris, Dead Space, Outer Worlds and X4, so I have experienced a lot of the aspects that Bethesda tries to cover in this game.

Overall it is a very traditional Bethesda game, but doesn't really live up to todays standards. The quests are slow, generic and repetitive. The characters arent that memoriable and unique and the lack of alien races doesn't seem to improve this issue. We have the classic stereotypes with Sarah as a Soldier and Sam as a Cowboy. The most memoriable character seems to be Vasco who is a robot with no story at all.

The colony building seems more limited than in Fallout 4 and you are stuck with the same modules even though you max out your skills - except for some upgrades to mining and some additional decorations.

Shipbuilding doesn't seem that exciting as the basic modules usually makes you end out with a sort of rocket shaped ship and in general the ship designs nudge you towards either a block or a rectangle due to the way the builder forces you to build the ship - the number of modules also seems very limited even though you mix and match between different manufacturers.

Ship combat is somewhat exciting, but you easily get ganged up on by pirates and the game lacks the finesse and flexibility in how you maneuver your craft such as in elite dangerous or X4. This means that space combat very easily becomes a slug fest. where you either target specific parts or have to use specific parts.

Enemy variety is a big issue as well as you have spacers, pirates, cultists and aliens. each have the same behavior and tactics as fallout 4 and are very easy to cheese. The gun play feel sluggish compared to other titles and the guns lack customizability in terms of how they look and feel in combat. For example the old earth rifle looks really weird compared to a normal springfield rifle which seems to be their inspiration. The varuun Starshard seems to be one of the best guns in the game, but it is limited what you can actually do to customize it.

Shipbuilding, colony building and weapon/suit crafting seems to be really important aspects of the game and they have designated quite the number of skills to these elements, but they seem lackluster compared to their importance.

Weapon and Suit variety is also an issue as most suits look the same, laser weapons are limited to orion, solstice and equinox while ballastic weapons have a lot of variety. The rarity system doesn't really make this better as you are constantly looking for the right mix of traits as normal weapons are kind of useless when playing on higher difficulties. the same for the suits.

Capacity is also a big issue in this game. The game wants you to pick up every ressource you find so you can upgrade, research and build, but you have very limited capacity. This leaves you with two options - either go back and forth between your spaceship/base or increase your capacity through the settings (if you have that as an option in your game you know it is bad!). suits, skills and food doesn't really solve this unless you change the setting, so you will spend a lot of time on traveling or constantly having low health.

Mods solve a lot of these issues and a lot of the story mods seems to be better structured and more engaging than the actual in game story - for example the cryomancer or farseer stories. mods that augments shipbuilding and add parts also makes up for this and mods that add different traits or upgrades to weapons and armor has also improved my game.

The only issue being that Bethesda is now taking money for these through their creations shop.

Overall i wouldn't recommend this game unless you want a fallout 4 in space, but with all the down sides of fallout turned up to the max as the game it self hasn't improved any mechanics beyond the graphics.

I WANTED to like this game. There's so many good aspects of this game where you can see the potential. The New Creation Engine is amazing, the features for gravity, shipbuilding, and space combat feel really good.

People will shit on the engine or the loading screen frequency or any NPC animations, but these are all shallow things that don't affect the actual quality of the game. They're not the problem.

The problem is the questline design, and nothing makes it more clear than those few questlines that are designed well: The UC Vanguard Questline. It's makes such good use of the new engine and mechanics, it has good writing, you can explore a lot of what this game CAN offer.

Then you play anything else, like the main quest. Get thing from planet, go back to New Atlantis. Go to new planet, come back again. They have a huge playground in space that they just don't use. They have a few populated planets each with only one city - a little immersion breaking but I understand the limitations. The problem is they keep making you go between planets for the most inane things. If you're focusing on a questline you rarely stay in one place for long, and when you travel somewhere else there's no excitement or danger: you go through a loading screen to travel then go through another loading screen and another. If it was a loading screen to space and then there was something to do in space before getting to your destination, that would be SOMETHING. The reason everyone points to the loading screens as a flaw isn't because separate cells are unbearable, it's because Bethesda treated most of this game like all their others where everything is one single continuous map with some interiors. The separated maps aren't the fatal flaw, they're merely the lens that exposes the flaw.

This COULD be a good game - if it utilized its own systems and tech upgrades, but it doesn't. The engine feels modern, but the gameplay loop most questlines thrust the player into hasn't caught up. It's a disjointed, incongruous experience that occasionally shows you a 10/10 experience hidden beneath a pile of mediocrity.

One more message specifically for Todd Howard: We play your old games because they're fun to REPLAY and try different builds or factions. Cutting off certain parts of the game for one character based on the player's choices does not limit player freedom, but rather increases and rewards it. Removing consequences from player's choices does not increase player freedom, it renders it meaningless. Stop taking the wrong lessons from your older successes.

Edit: I played 50 hours on gamepass, stop whining about the playtime, Steam is not all-knowing.

This is a time where steam really needs an ok review. I wouldn't say that this game is a do not buy. I would say it's a buy heavily discounted. I have 400+ hours in this and I really don't know how. Not in a "wow this was so fun I lost track of time." but in a I think I must've left it running and didn't realize it kind of way. Starfield isn't all bad. The exploration of space and the shipbuilder are very fun, and the combat is solid. The style and overall theme of the game is great. I mean a retro-futurism focused on NASA, what's not to love. The quests are strictly ok. With the exception of one notable quests involving some historical figures, most are entirely forgetable. That being said, that's where the praise ends. The pacing is odd, the story is weak at best, and the dialogue is abysmal. Touching more on the story, it feels like the entire story was written around the idea of having a new game plus and no thought was put into making it interesting or compelling.  Also, I'm not saying that every story has to be gritty and dark, but it feels like Starfield was sanitized so heavily to try and get a Teen rating to the point of being a bland milquetoast version of a game. Lastly, the "over 1000 planets". This was sold as one of the main points of the game. And yes, exploring the vastness of space is very fun, and yes most of space is empty in real life. However, it feels like they spent so much time on creating this vast expanse of space to explore and then they ran out of time to fill it with anything meaningful. There seems to be only a handful of layouts and designs for POIs and the few you find are far between. In a word: artless. Starfield feels like the natural endpoint of a studio that has been recycling the same approach for twenty years. Everything about it looks ambitious on paper, but the game itself feels like the result of blending scale, procedural generation, and AAA risk-aversion into something strangely empty.

I’ve wanted a proper space game for as long as I’ve been playing games. I love science fiction. I love the fantasy of exploring strange worlds, finding weird little corners of the galaxy, and getting lost in something that feels genuinely unknown. But I think I finally have to accept that this kind of game might never happen at the AAA level. Starfield made that clear.

Because the moment you load into your first planet, you feel the same problem that No Man’s Sky had at launch. When you rely on procedural generation to fill the gaps between handcrafted content, you end up with a lot of space and not a lot of meaning. A hundred empty planets don’t equal one memorable one. And when you try to balance both breadth and bespoke design, the seams show everywhere.

The sad part is that none of this is surprising. Not for Bethesda. Not for AAA.

Bethesda jank used to be charming because the games had personality. The bugs stood on top of something that felt alive. Starfield has the bugs, but the personality is gone. The worlds feel assembled rather than created. The systems feel like they exist because they were on a production roadmap. Ship building. Outposts. Crafting. Factions. A thousand tasks that all blend together into the same gray paste.

This is what happens when a massive team tries to satisfy every possible audience. Too many cooks. Too much money at stake. Too many shareholders who want a game that looks ambitious without taking any actual creative risks. 

The only perplexing thing about Starfield is why they made it at all. Maybe it was the classic trap. The scope was too big. The tech wasn’t ready. The premise demanded bespoke content on a cosmic scale, which is nearly impossible to execute in a way that feels meaningful. When you try to simulate an entire galaxy, you end up with something that feels like a diorama of one.

I wanted to like Starfield. I waited years. The problem isn't unique to Starfield, it's AAA in general. You either get a giant open world packed with shallow systems, or you get a highly scripted roller coaster that barely feels like a game. There’s very little in between.

The silver lining is that indie games are better than ever. Maybe that’s where the real experiments will keep happening. Maybe that’s where someone will finally make a space game worth getting lost in.

It just isn’t this one.

If I had to pick one word to use for Starfield, it would be "unfortunately". The core game is good, technology wise the game is the best yet aside from one minor bug I found very early that was easily resolved. The loading screens are an unfortunate result of the game engine's age, but the game looks pretty and you can get some really great views from it.

However this is not where the game falls down, for all it's technical accomplishments (and for the game engine, it really is especially the ship building stuff) the game is fatally holed by the universe. Someone hilariously and depressingly summed it up as "Space America vs Space Texas" and this couldn't be more true. The background lore is generally bland, and is disappointingly not expanded upon when it isn't. That's ignoring the bits that don't make sense under the mildest scrutiny.

The story's version of "exotic" is anyone with an accent, and they can veer too close to the stereotype sun, so it too often feels a bit uncomfortable or bordering on parody. The main companions are better, but there is too little variety in their outlook - what flavour of "Lawful Good" would you like today?

The main mission is terribly bland and like the rest of the game full to the brim with missed opportunities - why does each new universe mean so little? Why are there so many powers when most are rubbish and/or poorly explained? There was a golden opportunity to make comparisons with the Hunter as you - the player - start to see each universe as a stepping stone and become more detached from the people in it. Or even put the extra effort in for very minor visual changes each universe that help make it feel more meaningful. Can't even be bothered give a character a different hair style?

The game has a great visual feel to it (Space Texas aside), but even this lacks cohesion. There's some posters for war veterans getting cybernetic limbs - cool.  Is there any other mention of this, does anyone have a cybernetic limb? No. Planets look great, and seeing other planet and moons in the system doesn't get old. Sadly I can't say the same for how sparse all of them are, exploring to see the same thing you've seen countless times before.

The character customisation is good at its core, but - surprise - unfortunately it is let down by the clothing and suit options. You're really reduced in choice, with just a body and head for clothing and the space suit gets a backpack on top - there's no crafting just (reduced) upgrade options. Trying to get a decent suit set is like gambling as you raid chests and boss corpses hoping for something that doesn't suck (it will). That's before you want a matching set... Coming from other Bethesda games this is a huge downgrade and an even bigger let down. Fallout 4 had gibbing in, but that's missing too despite the bigger and nastier space guns here. Why are we getting so much less in a newer game?

The random POIs are good in theory, but there are far too few. I very quickly memorised them and knew where to look and what to find, it makes the game wear on you sooner than it should. There needs to be at least twice as many, ideally many more.

I'm going to summarise now, before this gets any longer and I write a small novel. To sum it up, Starfield feels like missed opportunity after missed opportunity coupled with too many downgrades over previous games. If you want to properly delve into a universe and feel part of it Starfield isn't going to do that and unfortunately that's what I want from my RPG games - I tried for too long to find it in Starfield.

I'll pick it up from time to time, as there is still enough to enjoy especially with mods (even if it's just killing the Space Pirates who are written so poorly I can't help but exterminate them every play through). Unfortunately that feels like the secret to enjoying Starfield - give up on most of the writing, characters, and factions (except the Vanguard and SysDef, best by far) - then you can enjoy the gameplay on its own. I suppose the Hunter was right all along.

This game doesn't know what it wants to be. Clearly, Bethesda was inspired by No Man's Sky but the open world nature of that game conflicts with Bethesda's strengths as a studio. The procedural generation of the planets results in content which commits the cardinal sin of gaming, which is that it is BORING. There are a few scattered points of interest, and some resources to gather and animals or plants to scan and that's basically it. NMS has all kinds of interesting things to find but not here. Plus the fact that you have to scan objects multiple times is just pointless busy work.

You do get the signature Bethesda RPG features like fully voice-acted dialog but, honestly, who cares? Who is actually listening to all of this? It worked in Skyrim because there are a lot more interesting characters and the world is more flavorful but here, IDK, I just did not really care about most of the characters I met and most of your companions are so goody two shoes and bland.

The combat is okay - it is serviceable at at least. Some of the extended quest lines are not bad. And the ship building is decent if kind of generic. My main issue with the gameplay is that Bethesda didn't commit to their own mechanics. You can mine and extract resources but they can all be bought so cheaply from basically anywhere that there is little point. You can build a base but your ship has all the features anyways so what is the point? And again, that's because the game doesn't know what it wants to be - it has some of the gathering-crafting mechanics of NMS but they feel relatively pointless. Some of the quest lines are pretty good but the core of the game is extremely generic and lazily implemented procedurally generated worlds which are boring and stale and just not fun to run around. In my opinion, it would have been better if they had concentrated on a more limited number of planets which were more densely populated with content and locations. This mish-mash of survival game, procedural generation, and hand-written quests just does not come together. It is like a bunch of disjointed parts that don't play well together.

And though I didn't ever get there, the NG+ mode is not a good fit for a game like this. You spend dozens of hours building bases and ships, finding the best gear, and doing all the quests and you want me to do it all over again, just with my better skills and abilities? Yeah, no thanks - I have no interest is resetting my progress. This is yet another feature that just seems tagged on which doesn't work well with the whole.

I will say that I did have some fun with this game and it has its merits. But for most of these boxes they were trying to check off here, you'd be better off playing No Man's Sky, which does "endless" space, procedural generation, and survival-crafting extremely well. There are also minimal loading screens - dear god, don't get me started with the ludicrous number of loading screens in Starfield. It's absurd.

It looks nice, and I do appreciate the "NASAcore" aesthetic, but there's just not a lot that's compelling in this game.
The main quest starts of okay, loses steam in the middle, and ends in a nonsensical way.
The companions you can have with you all have mostly flat personalities that didn't compel me to have any particular one stay with me.
The different planets are mostly barren randomly-generated wastelands, and that kills any real sense or desire for exploration.
The gameplay is basic but usable, generally what you expect from a Bethesda game.
Space flight/combat is cool, but is hardly present in the overall flow of the game, and the way travel from different locations works, you'll just end up fast-travelling most of the time anyway.
The non-randomly-generated locations are hit and miss, but some of them are actually pretty cool.
Building you own ship is actually relatively fun after you get used to the UI.
All in all the game is okay, but not worth the full price I paid for it, and I'm not excited for any DLC or sequels.
Disappointing game. Certainly not worth 70$. Maybe not worth your time.

Starfield is a poorly designed game, coupled with critical bugs that show an absolute disregard for the customers who purchased the game. 

Every encounter is with dozens of enemies who always have the high ground, and frequently surround you. When fighting at long range, the computer has perfect accuracy on shots, frequently ignores cover, and combines that with invisible walls that turn hits into misses every time. Enemies are also complete bullet sponges. 

This game's definition of "difficulty" is built around this combination of bugs left carefully in place, and conscious design decisions built around attritional difficulty. The game literally designs single encounters to run you out of medpacks. 

As with combat, exploration is tedium combined with unfixed bugs, 2 years after the game's release. Environmental hazards are jacked up such that getting out of your ship and walking 100 meters has you already taking damage. This is, again, combined with encounters of a dozen or so opponents, who have the high ground and their (I assume this is at least purposeful) unerring long-range accuracy. 

The combination of a bug causing the planet's environment to ignore my suit, and remove my boostpack, while simultaneously inflicting poison damage, while I was being attacked by a dozen zealots was on one of the first missions of the entire game. 

I am almost embarrassed to admit that I played this game to completion, because I had to see if it got better. This is the company that gave us Skyrim after all, one of my favorite games. I couldn't believe the game would actually stay THIS BAD.

In fact, the final mission in the game was actually worse. Enemies that can spawn endless duplicates of themselves (with rocket launchers, naturally), who teleport away every time you attack them, and run you through one shooting gallery after another (I believe there are six total shooting galleries) all in a bid to, again, run you out of healing. That's right, the game has MULTIPLE encounters like this. 

This game has that Bethesda magic in spots, as long as you are only doing procedurally generated missions. The moment you engage with either the main story, or a faction questline, you will be subjected to numerous attritional encounters, where bugs combine with stunningly bad, unfixed bugs. 

This game has no respect for you or your time, nor does it really seem to give a damn if you have fun. It is without a doubt the worst Bethesda game ever, and I have played every game they have developed since Morrowind. 

If you're considering buying this game on a holiday sale, as I did, do yourself a favor and skip it. No matter the price, you could find something better to spend it on.

Starfield is haunting.

It's a beautiful, expansive canvas, a labor of astonishing love for science-fiction, astronomy, and humanity. And upon this canvas is sketched the most bare framework of a game.

Or perhaps *stretched* is the better word; what's basically happened is that all the elements of Fallout 4 or Skyrim have been pulled apart, quite literally, and laid across a thousand planets rather than given context in their relative placement in a theme-park world, like previous Bethesda games. You aren't distracted and pulled from curious thing to strange location as you work your way toward an eventual destination, but instead hopping directly to wherever it is you "want" to go.

The lack of context really hurts the content on offer. Some of the best quest writing and environmental design in any Bethesda game is severely let down by its meaningless, randomized placement on otherwise dead worlds. The "lore" feels much more shallow because the cartoony character of the economics and politics at play is so much more obvious when planted in the middle of endless, unexploited wilderness.

And all of these problems are relatively minor in comparison to my real problem: the game feels like it's actively admonishing the player for playing it. The core conflict in the main story is set up to critique the same activities the game encourages the player to engage with... by being the *only* activities available. You will kill six thousand space pirates, whether or not it's logical that that many even exist, because you have no other choice if you want to play the game, and the game will call you evil for doing that. The ending will, incredibly, make this feel even worse.

A more constrained game could pull all this off. By assigning the player a character, or by narrowing the scope of their explorations, a more pleasant experience could be possible (and indeed has been, in games like Freelancer, Mass Effect, Rogue Trader, or Spec Ops: The Line). But Starfield intends to capture the eerie sensation of the desolate universe we find ourselves in, instead, and has tried to strap another game to that experience.

Starfield is haunting because it almost achieves what it sets out to do, and then hobbles itself. I can't help but imagine what it might've been.

All my waxing philosophical aside, you can get a couple hundred hours of decent fun out of this thing if you're willing to put up with some pain points. The combat is good! The environments are astonishing! There's a lot of cool things out there! They're just too far apart for most people to appreciate, and for every great quest there's a dozen of the same, identical outpost full of space pirates inexplicably having a picnic on an airless moon.
