Starfield is a poorly designed game, coupled with critical bugs that show an absolute disregard for the customers who purchased the game. 

Every encounter is with dozens of enemies who always have the high ground, and frequently surround you. When fighting at long range, the computer has perfect accuracy on shots, frequently ignores cover, and combines that with invisible walls that turn hits into misses every time. Enemies are also complete bullet sponges. 

This game's definition of "difficulty" is built around this combination of bugs left carefully in place, and conscious design decisions built around attritional difficulty. The game literally designs single encounters to run you out of medpacks. 

As with combat, exploration is tedium combined with unfixed bugs, 2 years after the game's release. Environmental hazards are jacked up such that getting out of your ship and walking 100 meters has you already taking damage. This is, again, combined with encounters of a dozen or so opponents, who have the high ground and their (I assume this is at least purposeful) unerring long-range accuracy. 

The combination of a bug causing the planet's environment to ignore my suit, and remove my boostpack, while simultaneously inflicting poison damage, while I was being attacked by a dozen zealots was on one of the first missions of the entire game. 

I am almost embarrassed to admit that I played this game to completion, because I had to see if it got better. This is the company that gave us Skyrim after all, one of my favorite games. I couldn't believe the game would actually stay THIS BAD.

In fact, the final mission in the game was actually worse. Enemies that can spawn endless duplicates of themselves (with rocket launchers, naturally), who teleport away every time you attack them, and run you through one shooting gallery after another (I believe there are six total shooting galleries) all in a bid to, again, run you out of healing. That's right, the game has MULTIPLE encounters like this. 

This game has that Bethesda magic in spots, as long as you are only doing procedurally generated missions. The moment you engage with either the main story, or a faction questline, you will be subjected to numerous attritional encounters, where bugs combine with stunningly bad, unfixed bugs. 

This game has no respect for you or your time, nor does it really seem to give a damn if you have fun. It is without a doubt the worst Bethesda game ever, and I have played every game they have developed since Morrowind. 

If you're considering buying this game on a holiday sale, as I did, do yourself a favor and skip it. No matter the price, you could find something better to spend it on.

Starfield is haunting.

It's a beautiful, expansive canvas, a labor of astonishing love for science-fiction, astronomy, and humanity. And upon this canvas is sketched the most bare framework of a game.

Or perhaps *stretched* is the better word; what's basically happened is that all the elements of Fallout 4 or Skyrim have been pulled apart, quite literally, and laid across a thousand planets rather than given context in their relative placement in a theme-park world, like previous Bethesda games. You aren't distracted and pulled from curious thing to strange location as you work your way toward an eventual destination, but instead hopping directly to wherever it is you "want" to go.

The lack of context really hurts the content on offer. Some of the best quest writing and environmental design in any Bethesda game is severely let down by its meaningless, randomized placement on otherwise dead worlds. The "lore" feels much more shallow because the cartoony character of the economics and politics at play is so much more obvious when planted in the middle of endless, unexploited wilderness.

And all of these problems are relatively minor in comparison to my real problem: the game feels like it's actively admonishing the player for playing it. The core conflict in the main story is set up to critique the same activities the game encourages the player to engage with... by being the *only* activities available. You will kill six thousand space pirates, whether or not it's logical that that many even exist, because you have no other choice if you want to play the game, and the game will call you evil for doing that. The ending will, incredibly, make this feel even worse.

A more constrained game could pull all this off. By assigning the player a character, or by narrowing the scope of their explorations, a more pleasant experience could be possible (and indeed has been, in games like Freelancer, Mass Effect, Rogue Trader, or Spec Ops: The Line). But Starfield intends to capture the eerie sensation of the desolate universe we find ourselves in, instead, and has tried to strap another game to that experience.

Starfield is haunting because it almost achieves what it sets out to do, and then hobbles itself. I can't help but imagine what it might've been.

All my waxing philosophical aside, you can get a couple hundred hours of decent fun out of this thing if you're willing to put up with some pain points. The combat is good! The environments are astonishing! There's a lot of cool things out there! They're just too far apart for most people to appreciate, and for every great quest there's a dozen of the same, identical outpost full of space pirates inexplicably having a picnic on an airless moon.

If you want a game with a compelling narrative, great gameplay, and pushes the medium of video games forward, avoid this, at all costs. Two of the faction quests are honestly my favourite Bethesda questlines ever, even if the writing has gotten a bit juvinile with clear good vs bad choices and a pathetic attempt at nuance.

But the main quest is shallow, repetative, and at odds with the established universe. Bethesda touts how immersive picking up a sandwich is while ignoring things like tactical reloads on guns or melee animations pulled straight out of Skyrim. Heck, in some ways, Skyrim was better, because you got that kill cam with unique animations! I'm not trying to be a combat nut here, but it is the core gameplay loop presented in this game. The world feels too empty where it should be crowded, and too crowded where it should feel empty. All but two of the "cities" feel like small backwaters, meanwhile every single one of the thousands of planets and moons is absolutely infested with abandoned research facilities and mines. That math ain't mathin. 

It's an odd game to talk about in detail. It feels wildly ambitious in some areas and then creatively bankrupt in others. It's got heart at times, and then can feel completely soulless other times.

I think if you're of the right personality, you can enjoy this game and sink a lot of time into it like I have (played the Games Pass version before the price hike). But I'm of the mentality that it's ok to enjoy a bad game. Just like how popcorn is bad for you, and not particularly exceptional in taste. You can still enjoy it as a snack.

Starfield is a failure of a game made by a company riding on it's past success, this just isn't the same company that made The Elder Scrolls games. The exploration of this game was just tedious and uninteresting. There is not an open area of that allows you to travel planet to planet. They are, separate, isolated, open game areas that have invisible walls in every direction that lead to nowhere. The game about exploring outer space, does not actually have any aspect that lets you travel and explore through space. Almost all of the traversal through "space" is loading screens and maps. It is completely avoidable and I felt practically incentivized to do so. Planets are empty gigantic open areas of seemingly random mishmash. Most of them aren't even worth visiting as quite literally nothing is going on inside of them. Npcs are horribly uncanny and stiff, not to mention their behavior in general being non-sensical. The members of Constellation all feel weirdly thrust onto the player as strangers pretending to know you. Constellation as an organization doesn't even have you exploring space because you literally can't. City Environments feel baren and empty, New Atlantis is basically just a handful of stores placed across a giant empty floor. Akila City, Neon, and other areas occupied by humans but look noticeably un-inhabited. Outposts as a system is so unintuitive and frustrating the gameplay experience is better if you just completely forget about it. To emphasize, when you ignore it you miss absolutely nothing it had to offer. Combat felt like roadblocks on the way to floating quest markers. Hostile Npcs are all suicidal, they absolutely have zero regard for their own lives. Most of them running out from cover, into the open, and closing the gap between the player just to stare at them before letting off one or two missed shots point blank. Ship combat lacks any kind of engaging gameplay, all interesting avenues outer space combat could of had are completely discarded. Space combat is just a random event that inconvenience's you on the way into a planet.  The large variety of guns somehow all feel similar, with even less customization than Fallout 4. The art direction is boring, bland, and not memorable whatsoever. The story is a long series of events with zero consequence. The twist at the end? You get to experience this slog all over again.

If you are looking for a space exploration themed game, coming directly from the Elders Scrolls series or the acquired Fallout series of Bethesda as a fan of those games and their mechanics, you may like this.  That being said, it is absolutely no different than Fallout or Elder Scrolls, with the exception of the setting.  This is literally Skyrim in space.  Do yourself a favor, play a better game if space exploration is your thing.  Hell, if RPGs are your thing, let me do you a better favor, stay away from Bethesda RPGs.  It's fundamentally an open ended, open world beat-em-up/hack-and-slash where in the end you become a god like entity.. just like all of all the other productions.  If you're looking for a true RPG, this isn't it.  If you're looking for a mindless point and shoot adventure, this is the one.

Just go play Fallout or Skyrim.
